Gray catalysts with unclear implications sustain this by attracting opposing views until capital constraints force transactions. Examples include COVID in March 2020 where dip buyers and vol sellers fueled further declines, and meme mania in January 2021 with GameStop and AMC where shorts added fuel to the surge.

text:
By nature of being a vol trader, I’ve studied many different market crashes. Not just the common ones in the U.S., but episodes like Britain in 1720, Vienna in 1873, and the Dutch tulip mania of 1637.

There are some interesting behavioral takeaways that aren’t entirely intuitive unless you participate in markets every single day.

One of the biggest for me is that large market moves often need two-way action to develop. Behaviorally, you need participants willing to take the other side, because their eventual need to unwind can help accelerate the move. It’s almost like storing energy that gets released later. To create that dynamic, a “gray catalyst” can be particularly powerful one whose implications aren’t immediately black and white. 

Here are two examples that helped produce massive moves in opposite directions that had gray area headlines that led to that two way flow. 

COVID (March 2020): What often gets lost in the sauce is that many participants were aggressively betting against the idea that COVID would be severely disruptive. As stocks fell, they bought the dip and sold vol. When stocks kept falling and vol kept rising, some of those positions became fuel for the next leg of the move as participants were forced to unwind.

Looking back, the outcome seems obvious. In real time, the eventual scale of the disruption was far from clear. There was HOPE that it would pass quickly. Headlines about potential treatments, policy support, or a less severe impact repeatedly

text:
THE BORING COMPANY HQ: Bastrop, Texas, October

Here is my flyover of TBC's Bastrop headquarters and Prufrock factory. It's is where they test every machine before it ships, build and store equipment, precast tunnel segments, liner trucks, vertical cassettes and conveyor belt systems, and more. They house their Prufrock Command Center here to control all the Prufrock's soon to be around the world.

- The SpaceX Pedestrian Tunnel started as Porpoise Test 6 (PT6). TBC first bored it to test (no people in the tunnel) ZPIT continuous mining, an upgraded liner truck and the "SNAILS on RAILS" navigation system. After the test, they turned it into a 500 ft walkway under FM1209 that connects the SpaceX site to Hyperloop Plaza, where The Boring Bodega is. People use it so they don't have to cross that busy road on foot.
 
- Hard-rock Prufrock-MB4 being constructed for Nashville's Music City LOOP.

- The Test Tunnel PT5 connects SpaceX's Starlink factory to TBC under FM1209. It was the first use of custom hexagonal segments, automated gantry steering, quick craneless retrieval, and the first version of ZPIT. It's now a test bench for liner trucks, vertical cassettes and new belt systems.

- Hyperloop Test Tunnel was PT4; the first craneless, pitless retrieval of the machine. It's now a vacuum tunnel for Hyperloop vacuum pump system testing. It also connects SpaceX's Starlink factory to TBC under FM1209.

- Always positive to hear from

This spin even made the lead story on the front page of The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday: “More Oil Is Now Coming Out of the Persian Gulf Than Before the Iran War.”

The narrative just didn’t make any sense. If there is so much oil coming out of the Strait, why does the price of Brent keep hitting new highs with each passing day? Two plus two does not equal five.

After the most recent price surge, Trump was forced to switch stories. On his social media platform, Truth Social, he threw in the towel on high prices and is now blaming them on Iran. But this narrative makes absolutely no sense either, since it was Trump’s war of choice against Iran that made the Strait functionally inoperative and caused the price of Brent to soar by 60% since the start of the war.

name: Kris Sidial🇺🇸
zh_summary: @Ksidiii: short interest charts miss the flows: most shops are not making outright short bets; banks providing balance sheet for speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure to ease margin requirements.
en_summary: @Ksidiii: short interest charts miss the flows: most shops are not making outright short bets; banks providing balance sheet for speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure to ease margin requirements.
text:
Everyone who keeps sharing these short interest charts is missing the flows behind them. Most shops are not taking outright short bets. This is another effort to ease margin requirements across the street: banks providing balance sheet for more speculative bets are asking clients to post more short exposure.

The sequence on the street looks like this:

HF manager: “I want more margin.”

Bank: “Things look risky in public AI bets, and we’re already lending a lot against private AI bets. For some clients, we’ll extend more financing, but only if they add more short exposure to improve their collateral scores.”

HF manager: “Okay, I’ll short more stock against my main bet.”

That is how you end up with short exposures that look astronomically high while many end users remain heavily long tech. The additional shorts are supporting the financing of their main bets.

Which also tells the bigger story on why raw equity financing rates haven’t blown out the way they did ahead of the big SpaceX IPO in June, despite the fact that lending is slowing.

text:
In early 2002, Elon was preparing to launch SpaceX and searching for the people who could help him build a rocket from scratch. One Sunday in January 2002, he walked into a friend's rented warehouse in Huntington Beach and found Tom Mueller holding an 80-pound rocket engine on his shoulder, trying to bolt it to a frame. It was the largest liquid-fuel engine any amateur had ever built, with 13,000 pounds of thrust, made in Tom's spare time. 

Elon asked the main question  “Could you build something bigger?”

The next Sunday Elon came to his house. It was Super Bowl Sunday; they watched maybe one play, because they were too busy sketching the first SpaceX rocket.

Tom became SpaceX employee #1, and the man who built engines on weekends went on to build Merlin, Kestrel and Draco. 

Elon saw a person, not a résumé, someone who built rockets with his own hands simply because he loved them.

name: Puru Saxena
zh_summary: Puru Saxena notes that drawdowns are normal for the S&P 500, with ~80-95% of time below prior peaks historically, and advises staying the course for long-term equity returns as volatility is the price of admission.
en_summary: Puru Saxena notes that drawdowns are normal for the S&P 500, with ~80-95% of time below prior peaks historically, and advises staying the course for long-term equity returns as volatility is the price of admission.
text:
Drawdowns are the norm. New highs are the exception.

Historically the S&P 500 has spent ~80–95% of its time below a prior peak. Since 1871, 82% of months were underwater (price basis). Since 1950, only about 7% of trading days were at record highs.

Volatility is the price of admission. You cannot earn equity-like long-term returns with bond-like volatility; there is no free lunch. The temporary discomfort of being below your high-water mark is the cost of capturing the upside over decades.

That’s why staying the course matters for investors:

• Markets trend higher over time, but the path is jagged. Recoveries eventually erase most drawdowns. 
• Selling during declines locks in losses and risks missing the rebound. 
• The bigger risk is interrupting compounding by trying to avoid normal volatility.

Being underwater is uncomfortable but expected. The investors who do best treat drawdowns as the entry fee, not a reason to exit. Stay invested and let the long-term maths work.

“Jason, I think 10 days is too long. I think these things are going to happen much faster than every 10 days.

I think part of the challenge we're seeing is we've been talking about technology debt that we all have to pay sooner than later.

And what's happened is people have not paid attention to the idea that they have to go fix their stuff.

We found out about this a few days ago. We've scanned everything in our infrastructure to make sure that there were no issues. We made sure that our products had patches available for our customers who deploy them.

So there's two ways to solve this problem, right?

One, you can go in and patch the vulnerability. You can go in, find the code, patch what has been given to you by PHP, and make it work.

The other is you can actually put it in a perimeter defense product like ours, or Cloudflare has one, or other firewalls have one.

If you put the patch there, it's a virtual patch, so any attacker trying to access that vulnerability gets stopped at the perimeter because we know what they're looking for.

Guess what? The phones keep ringing every day, and the conversation always is, ‘Now how do I get out of this? Because I'm tired of getting punched in the face every morning when I wake up.’”
